title: What load-balancing algorithms exist (round robin, least connections, least response time, IP hash / sticky sessions, weighted, consistent hashing), and when do you use each?
shortTitle: What load-balancing algorithms exist, and when do you use each?

s1_definition.profdef: Load-balancing algorithms decide which backend instance receives each incoming request. Round robin cycles through instances in order, ideal for uniform requests and equal instances. Least connections sends each request to the instance with the fewest active connections, good when request durations vary. Least response time picks the instance with the lowest observed latency, good when instances differ in speed. IP hash (and sticky sessions) always sends a given client to the same instance, needed when the instance holds client-specific local state. Weighted variants assign more traffic to more powerful instances. Consistent hashing maps requests to instances via a hash ring so that adding or removing an instance remaps only a small fraction of keys, essential for distributed caches and sharded stores.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the floor manager at National Bank of India assigning arriving customers to teller windows. Round robin is "next customer to the next window in order" — simple and fair when every request is similar. Least connections is "send the next customer to the window with the shortest queue right now" — better when some customers take five minutes and others take an hour. Least response time is "send them to the window that has been serving fastest lately." IP hash or sticky sessions is "Mr. Rajesh always goes to window three because that teller is holding his half-finished paperwork." Weighted is "the senior teller's window gets more customers because they work faster." Consistent hashing is a smart seating chart where opening or closing one window only reshuffles a few customers instead of the whole hall.
s1_definition.oneliner: Pick round robin for uniform equal instances, least connections for variable request lengths, least response time for uneven instances, sticky or IP hash when local state ties a client to an instance, weighted for unequal capacity, and consistent hashing when instances come and go and you must minimize remapping.

**Professional definition:** Load-balancing algorithms decide which backend instance receives each incoming request. Round robin cycles through instances in order, ideal for uniform requests and equal instances. Least connections sends each request to the instance with the fewest active connections, good when request durations vary. Least response time picks the instance with the lowest observed latency, good when instances differ in speed. IP hash (and sticky sessions) always sends a given client to the same instance, needed when the instance holds client-specific local state. Weighted variants assign more traffic to more powerful instances. Consistent hashing maps requests to instances via a hash ring so that adding or removing an instance remaps only a small fraction of keys, essential for distributed caches and sharded stores.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the floor manager at National Bank of India assigning arriving customers to teller windows. Round robin is "next customer to the next window in order" — simple and fair when every request is similar. Least connections is "send the next customer to the window with the shortest queue right now" — better when some customers take five minutes and others take an hour. Least response time is "send them to the window that has been serving fastest lately." IP hash or sticky sessions is "Mr. Rajesh always goes to window three because that teller is holding his half-finished paperwork." Weighted is "the senior teller's window gets more customers because they work faster." Consistent hashing is a smart seating chart where opening or closing one window only reshuffles a few customers instead of the whole hall.

**One line to remember:** Pick round robin for uniform equal instances, least connections for variable request lengths, least response time for uneven instances, sticky or IP hash when local state ties a client to an instance, weighted for unequal capacity, and consistent hashing when instances come and go and you must minimize remapping.

sections.s2_technical:
Round robin distributes requests by cycling through the instance list in order: first request to instance A, second to B, third to C, then back to A. It is simple, stateless, and fair when every request costs about the same and every instance is equally powerful. A small example is keeping an index and doing `instances.get(index++ % instances.size())`. Its weakness is that it ignores actual load, so if one request happens to be very expensive, the instance that got it is now overloaded while round robin keeps sending it more.

Least connections sends each new request to the instance currently handling the fewest active connections. This adapts to reality: if one instance is bogged down by long-running requests, its connection count stays high and it receives fewer new requests. It is the right default when request durations vary widely, which they usually do in real systems. The balancer must track live connection counts per instance, so it is slightly more stateful than round robin.

Least response time picks the instance with the lowest recently measured response latency, often combined with connection count. This is best when instances are not equally fast — maybe some run on slower hardware or in a busier zone — because it routes toward whichever is actually serving quickest. It requires the balancer to continuously measure per-instance latency.

IP hash and sticky sessions both aim to pin a client to a consistent instance. IP hash computes a hash of the client's IP and maps it to an instance, so the same client consistently lands on the same one. Sticky sessions achieve the same using a cookie the balancer sets. You use these only when the instance holds client-specific local state, such as an in-memory session, so the client must return to the instance that has their data. The important caveat is that stickiness undermines even load distribution and breaks if that instance dies, which is why the better long-term fix is usually to externalize state so you do not need stickiness at all.

Weighted variants (weighted round robin, weighted least connections) assign a weight to each instance proportional to its capacity, so a more powerful instance receives proportionally more traffic. You use this when instances are deliberately unequal, for example during a gradual rollout where a new larger instance type should take more load, or a canary that should take only a small slice.

Consistent hashing maps both instances and request keys onto a hash ring, and each key is served by the next instance clockwise on the ring. Its defining property is that when you add or remove an instance, only the keys in that instance's arc are remapped — roughly one over N of the keys — instead of nearly all keys being reshuffled as happens with plain modulo hashing. This is essential for distributed caches and sharded data stores, where remapping a key means a cache miss or a data move, so you want to minimize churn when the instance set changes. Virtual nodes are added so each physical instance appears at many points on the ring, smoothing out the distribution.

The senior nuance is that the algorithm choice follows the workload. For stateless, uniform web requests behind equal instances, round robin or least connections is fine. For a distributed cache or sharded store, consistent hashing is almost mandatory. For anything that forces stickiness, treat it as a smell and prefer externalizing state. Weighted algorithms are for heterogeneous fleets and controlled rollouts. And crucially, every algorithm must be combined with health checks so dead instances are removed from rotation, because distributing traffic evenly to a dead instance is worse than useless.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India's API tier has several backend instances, and different services need different balancing strategies.

Problem 1 — The uneven tellers. The statement-generation service had requests that varied wildly: some statements were one page, some were a thousand pages. Round robin kept sending new big requests to an already-busy instance. This is exactly where least connections wins — route to whoever has the shortest live queue.

Problem 2 — The cache that thrashed. The balance-cache tier used plain modulo hashing to pick a cache node. When one node was added for scaling, nearly every key remapped, every lookup became a cache miss, and the database was hammered. This is exactly the problem consistent hashing solves — adding a node remaps only a small fraction of keys.

We will model a `LoadBalancer` abstraction with several strategies: round robin, least connections, and consistent hashing, each selecting a backend for a request. The demo shows round robin cycling, least connections avoiding a busy instance, and consistent hashing remapping only a few keys when a node is added.

The code will have a `Backend`, a `LoadBalancingStrategy` interface, `RoundRobin`, `LeastConnections`, and `ConsistentHashing` implementations, and a demo that routes requests through each and prints the choices, including the before-and-after of adding a node under consistent hashing.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a pool of api-1, api-2, api-3; then api-1 made busy; then five account keys with a node added.

Step 1 — Round robin routes four requests. It cycles api-1, api-2, api-3, then back to api-1 — purely positional, ignoring how busy each instance is. This is fine only because the requests are assumed uniform.

Step 2 — Least connections runs with api-1 artificially busy (5 active) and api-3 idle (0 active). The big statement request goes to api-3, the least loaded, not to api-1. The algorithm adapted to real load instead of blindly cycling.

Step 3 — Consistent hashing builds a ring from api-1, api-2, api-3 with virtual nodes. Each account key maps to the first node clockwise on the ring. Five keys get assigned, and we record the before mapping.

Step 4 — We add api-4 to the ring. Because consistent hashing only remaps keys that fall into the new node's arc, only a small number of keys move; the rest stay on their original nodes. The demo counts how many remapped and notes that plain modulo hashing would have remapped almost all of them.

Step 5 — The contrast across strategies is clear: round robin is positional and load-blind, least connections is load-aware, and consistent hashing is churn-minimizing when the node set changes, which is why each suits a different situation.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Request / key
    │
    ▼
  LoadBalancingStrategy.pick(key)
    │
    ├─ RoundRobin ──────▶ idx++ % N          (positional, load-blind)
    │
    ├─ LeastConnections ▶ min(active count)  (load-aware)
    │       api-1(5) api-2(1) api-3(0) → choose api-3
    │
    └─ ConsistentHashing▶ hash ring, next node clockwise
            ring: ...api-2..api-1..api-3..  (virtual nodes smooth it)
            add api-4 → only keys in api-4's arc remap (≈1/N)
    │
    ▼
  Chosen backend  (+ health check must exclude dead instances)
```

```
  ═══ HLD — Choosing a Load-Balancing Algorithm per Tier ═══

  Clients ──▶ ┌──────────────────────┐
              │ Edge LB               │  least_conn (variable API durations)
              └──────────┬───────────┘
                 ┌───────┼────────┐
                 ▼       ▼        ▼
             api-1    api-2     api-3   (stateless → round robin also fine)

  Session tier (if stateful) ──▶ ip_hash / sticky  (pin client to instance)
     better: externalize session to Redis → then any algorithm works

  Cache / sharded store ──▶ CONSISTENT HASHING (ring + virtual nodes)
     add/remove node → only ≈1/N keys remap → minimal cache misses / data moves

  Heterogeneous fleet / canary ──▶ WEIGHTED (bigger box or canary gets a set share)

  ALWAYS pair with health checks: a dead instance must leave the rotation.
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Load-balancing algorithms decide which backend instance serves each request, and the right choice follows the workload. Round robin simply cycles through instances in order; it is simple and fair when requests are uniform and instances are equal, but it is load-blind, so if one request is very expensive, round robin keeps piling more onto the instance that got it. Least connections sends each request to the instance with the fewest active connections, which adapts to reality and is my default when request durations vary widely, because a busy instance naturally receives fewer new requests. Least response time goes further and routes toward whichever instance is actually serving fastest, which is best when instances are not equally powerful.

IP hash and sticky sessions both pin a client to a consistent instance, IP hash by hashing the client address and sticky sessions by a cookie. I use these only when an instance holds client-specific local state such as an in-memory session, but I treat the need for stickiness as a smell, because it undermines even distribution and breaks when that instance dies, so the better long-term fix is to externalize the state and drop stickiness entirely. Weighted variants assign more traffic to more powerful instances, which I use for heterogeneous fleets or controlled rollouts like canaries.

Consistent hashing maps both instances and keys onto a hash ring, and each key is served by the next instance clockwise. Its defining property is that adding or removing an instance only remaps the keys in that instance's arc, roughly one over N of them, instead of reshuffling almost everything the way plain modulo hashing does. That is essential for distributed caches and sharded stores, where a remapped key means a cache miss or a data move, and I add virtual nodes so each physical instance appears at many points on the ring for an even spread. In my bank I used least connections for the variable-length statement service and consistent hashing for the balance-cache tier, where adding a node used to remap nearly every key and hammer the database until consistent hashing limited the churn.

The principle I always close with is that every algorithm must be paired with health checks so a dead instance leaves the rotation, because distributing traffic evenly onto a dead instance is worse than useless.

The one-line summary I give is: round robin for uniform equal instances, least connections for variable request lengths, least response time for uneven instances, sticky or IP hash only when local state ties a client to an instance, weighted for unequal capacity or canaries, and consistent hashing when instances come and go and you must minimize remapping — always with health checks.
